title_html: ☆ Behave Like Experts: Fusing Data with Semantic Knowledge for Effective and Efficient Semantic Map Construction
authors_html: Zhu Liu, Zhen Hu, Yuxuan Liu, Ying Liu
summary: Semantic map models (SMMs) construct a graph that reflects conceptual similarity by comparing cross-lingual form-meaning mappings. Experts build such models not only by obeying the data constraint, i.e., the connectivity hypothesis, which states that conceptual nodes belonging to the same form must be connected, but also by incorporating their prior semantic knowledge. Current automatic methods ignore this knowledge, which harms both accuracy and efficiency by enlarging the search space of candidate graphs. In this paper, we fuse the distributional semantic knowledge hidden in the internal representations of language models into a top-down, data-driven algorithm. This expert-like behavior re-sorts the candidates in a huge search space, guided by conceptual semantics similarity. Experiments on a self-collected benchmark of 10 datasets and comprehensive metrics show that our method builds SMMs both effectively and efficiently.

title_html: ☆ Generation-Heavy Hybrid Machine Translation
authors_html: Nizar Yahya Habash
summary: The state of the art techniques in Machine Translation (MT) require large amounts of symmetric resources from source and target languages. This is true regardless of whether the approach is Transfer or Interlingua, Symbolic or Statistical. Symmetry within these approaches is necessary to ensure quality, robustness and retargetability. In reality, such symmetry, whether it is in terms of structural transfer lexicons, interlingual dictionaries or parallel corpora, is a major bottleneck in developing any MT system. This dissertation presents an approach to MT that addresses the lack of symmetry by exploiting symbolic and statistical target language resources in source-poor/target-rich language pairs. This approach is called Generation-Heavy Hybrid Machine Translation (GHMT). Expected source language resources include a syntactic parser and a simple one-to-many translation dictionary. No transfer rules or complex interlingual representations are used. Rich target language symbolic resources are used to overgenerate multiple structural variations from a target-glossed syntactic dependency representation of source language sentences. Statistical target-language resource are then used to select amongst the overgenerated translations. The source-target asymmetry of systems developed in this approach makes them more easily retargetable to new source languages.
comment: Dissertation submitted to the Faculty of the Graduate School of the University of Maryland at College Park in partial fulfillment of the requirements for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy 2003

title_html: ☆ Deep Fusion Memory: A Chunk-Level Parametric Memory for Large Language Models
authors_html: Rubin Wei, Siyuan Sun, Hao Sun, Yuliang Liu, Xiang Shi, Jiarui Wang, Junming Zhang, Zhouhan Lin
summary: Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. We introduce Deep Fusion Memory (DFM), a parametric memory architecture that reduces this construction workload and incorporates learned memory into intermediate hidden states. A causal memory predictor learns to generate memory from the preceding context, using retrieved chunk embeddings from the corpus as supervision. The predicted memory is shared across tokens within each chunk and fused into their hidden states through gated cross-attention. Memory prediction and fusion are trained end to end with the backbone frozen, and inference requires no explicit retrieval. Compared with existing parametric memory approaches, which often construct token-level memory targets, DFM requires $32\times$ fewer retrieval queries and $2048\times$ fewer retrieved items to construct its training data. Across six QA tasks, DFM performs better over the strongest baseline by 12.71% on Mistral-7B-v0.3 and 11.19% on Qwen3-8B-Base. Beyond QA, domain adaptation yields average gains of 6.51 and 4.38 points over Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base, respectively.

title_html: ☆ Beyond Factual Accuracy: A Benchmark for Evaluating Perspective Alignment in LLMs
authors_html: Sunghoon Kim, Sangyeop Kim
summary: Large Language Models often generate factually correct responses that fail to maintain user-requested perspectives, blending multiple perspectives and forcing users to filter through unwanted information---a perspective control failure that factual accuracy metrics cannot detect. We introduce PerspectiveBench, a benchmark quantifying perspective alignment by constructing scenarios where multiple valid reasoning paths coexist, and propose the Perspective Alignment Score (PAS) to measure adherence to specified perspectives. Experiments reveal that state-of-the-art models successfully include target content but fail to exclude non-requested perspectives. Providing documents through RAG improves factual grounding but does not resolve perspective drift, as models prioritize comprehensive coverage over strict user constraints. Code and data are available at https://github.com/sunghoon014/PerspectiveBench.

title_html: ☆ Dual-Slot: From Serial Loops to Parallel Slots in Language Models
authors_html: Yiqin Hao, Zitong Wang, Boyi Zeng, He Li, Shixiang Song, Feichen Song, Yifan Liu, Zhouhan Lin
summary: Looped language models increase computational depth by repeatedly applying shared layers, offering a way to improve model quality without adding parameters. However, sequential dependencies between loop iterations increase autoregressive decoding latency. We introduce Dual-Slot, an architecture that reorganizes serial looped computation into parallel latent and prediction slots. Rather than waiting for the current token's latent computation to finish, the prediction slot combines the previous token's deep latent state with the current representation, while the latent slot produces a state for the next decoding step. This shifts the latent dependency across adjacent tokens, replacing two sequential module invocations with a single paired invocation while preserving standard autoregressive generation. To preserve token-level parallelism during training, we use a small number of Jacobi iterations to refine latent states across the sequence in parallel. Experiments on Qwen-style dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models show consistent improvements in language modeling and average downstream accuracy. On the 1B dense model, Dual-Slot reduces Pile validation perplexity from 7.25 to 7.00 and improves average five-shot accuracy across nine task configurations by 2.26 percentage points. After supervised fine-tuning, it improves zero-shot GSM8K accuracy by 5.83 and 3.49 percentage points for the 1B dense and A0.6B MoE models, respectively. Across the evaluated batch sizes, Dual-Slot retains 93.1-96.5% of vanilla decoding throughput for the dense model and 98.1-99.6% for the MoE model.
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures

title_html: ☆ P2N: Reusing Deep Representations for Greater Effective Depth
authors_html: Yiqin Hao, Boyi Zeng, Zitong Wang, He Li, Shixiang Song, Feichen Song, Yifan Liu, Zhouhan Lin
summary: Mathematical problem solving and autonomous agents are increasingly important applications of language models, demanding stronger reasoning capabilities. Computational depth is a key resource for such reasoning, but adding model layers increases both training and inference costs, while test-time scaling incurs substantial additional inference computation. We introduce P2N (Previous to Next), which reuses the previous token's deep representations, already available during generation, to increase effective computational depth with negligible decoding overhead. Specifically, P2N adds the previous token's deep hidden state to the current token's shallow representation, allowing subsequent layers to build on previously completed deep computation. This recurrence extends effective computational depth across tokens, while introducing only a single vector addition per decoding step. We train the recurrence using parallel Jacobi updates restricted to a middle-layer core. Experiments with Qwen-style models show that, at 1.5B parameters, P2N improves GSM8K accuracy by over 10 percentage points under both zero-shot and few-shot prompting, with nearly unchanged decoding latency. The benefits also extend to language modeling and average performance on general downstream benchmarks. on general downstream benchmarks.
comment: 23 pages, 10 figures

title_html: ☆ One Head Away from Language Confusion: Single Attention Heads Across Model Families
authors_html: Jiwon Jeong, Anjelo Jann Laroza, Chaewoon Yoon, Arjun Pillai, Pranav Kokati, Christian Hoang, Seunghyeok Hong
summary: Large language models sometimes reply in an unexpected language, a failure known as language confusion. We ablate individual attention heads in 12 model checkpoints spanning seven model series, using FLORES-200 continuations in five languages and Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB) chat replies. In ten models, zeroing one head causes substantially more departures from the expected language than zeroing any other head in its layer; its LCB pass-rate drop persists, though reduced, under mean ablation. Seven heads move 8.0 to 51.5 percent of all FLORES continuations out of the prompt's language, versus at most 1.4 percent for other same-layer heads; the other three mainly affect explicitly requested languages. These seven heads matter less in base models given plain text. In two models, replacing the values a head reads at the requested-language name with another language's mean makes replies fail and shifts some into that language, unlike a random change of equal size. Replacing a head's output with another language's mean redirects 84 to 99 percent of scored non-English monolingual LCB replies into that language in five models. Yet the requested language's mean improves crosslingual replies beyond every control head only in the two Gemma models, whose baselines are low. Code and results are available in the public repository at https://github.com/christian-hoang-04/anonymous-release.

title_html: ☆ When Does Better Acceptance Pay? A Controlled Study of Speculative Decoding
authors_html: Yongchao Long, Chunrui Zheng, Yuxuan Zhou, Guangkun Nie, Tian-Chi Ma, Chao Pang, Shuohuan Wang, Yuchen Ding, Xianbin Wen, Dianhai Yu, Junyuan Shang, Yuxi Zhou, Shenda Hong
summary: The throughput gains of speculative decoding depend on the trade-off between acceptance length and execution latency. We ask when additional acceptance is worth the cost of obtaining it. We establish a comparison protocol spanning training, inference, and evaluation, remeasuring released checkpoints and retraining six drafter recipes on shared target-generated data across ten benchmarks and two target models. Alignment changes the picture: gaps that appear large in published comparisons shrink substantially under shared training and inference conditions. This narrowing motivates two deeper questions: how is acceptance improved at different costs, and when do these gains improve throughput? We find that acceptance can be improved through nearly free objective and context changes or more expensive token-to-token conditioning. DCore illustrates the former route as a strong baseline with little additional measured drafting overhead. The payoff is conditional: task uncertainty and serving conditions affect acceptance returns, execution costs, and the preferred drafter and budget. These findings inform future drafter design and deployment choices.
comment: 24 pages, 11 figures. Project page: this https URL

title_html: ☆ The World as Viewed by 136 Countries: An Open, Curated, Annotated, and Multilingual Dataset of 118 Million State Media Articles
authors_html: Bryan Li, Samar Haider, Grace Kim, Fiona Luo, Jinqi Luo, Yuan Yuan, Duncan Watts, René Vidal, Chris Callison-Burch
summary: State media outlets often project their governments' narratives to target both domestic and foreign audiences. Because this content is plentiful and free to access, it appears widely in the web corpora that large language models (LLMs) are trained on and that retrieval systems draw from. However, the prevalence of state media in these corpora and its potential influence on LLM outputs remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce WorldStateMedia, an open dataset of 118 million state media articles from 136 countries in 114 languages. We extract these articles from existing pretraining corpora and annotate each outlet with level of state control from State Media Monitor. Using WorldStateMedia to audit these corpora, we find that, in English web crawls, the share of state media pages from editorially controlled (vs. independent) outlets rose from 39% in 2013 to 93% in 2025. In several low-resource languages, state media make up a substantial share of all web data, such as 17.8% for Uyghur and 7.8% for Belarusian. To characterize the differing narratives of news outlets, we compare Russian and Ukrainian state media in English and in their native languages, revealing asymmetric topical focus and opposing framings of contested issues such as Crimea. Furthermore, in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) experiment on territorial disputes, retrieving a country's state media shifts model answers toward that country's claims, most strongly for English-language (foreign-targeted) media. We release WorldStateMedia to support multilingual, cross-national insights on state media at https://huggingface.co/collections/manestay/worldstatemedia

title_html: ☆ A Measurement Perspective on Benchmarking LLM-Generated Text Detectors using Item Response Theory
authors_html: Yanbin Zhao, Zhipeng Chen, Guangsheng Bao, Guandong Zhang, Yan Li
summary: Benchmarking large language model (LLM)-generated text detectors commonly relies on aggregate detector-level metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, and AUC. Although useful for summarizing overall performance, these metrics provide limited insight into how benchmark composition shapes detector comparisons or which texts distinguish detectors with different response profiles. We propose a measurement-based benchmarking framework for jointly characterizing benchmark heterogeneity and detector behavior using multidimensional item response theory (IRT). By treating benchmark texts as measurement items and detectors as respondents, the framework estimates text-level discrimination and difficulty-location parameters alongside multidimensional detector abilities. We apply the framework to a benchmark of 32K human-written and machine-generated texts across four domains, evaluated by 14 detectors. The estimated IRT item-parameter space reveals distinct but overlapping human-machine distributions, with substantial variation across domains and text lengths. The human-machine label shows the strongest multivariate association with this space, while domain and text length further contribute to benchmark heterogeneity. Detector ability profiles reveal multidimensional and domain-dependent response patterns that are not fully reflected in aggregate performance rankings. As a practical application, clustering texts in the estimated IRT space yields a compact subset of 2,088 texts (6.5\% of the full 32K benchmark) that largely preserves the comparative detector-performance patterns observed on the full benchmark. Overall, the proposed framework provides a principled and interpretable methodology for benchmarking heterogeneous detection technologies while jointly characterizing the measurement properties of the texts used for their evaluation.

title_html: ☆ Rubrics Carry the Standard: Shapley Attribution for Checklist-Based LLM Judges
authors_html: Saeid Asgari, Rui Ying, Sara Malvar, Rakshanda Agarwal, Bruce Sun, Claire Wang, Leonardo de Oliveira Nunes, Ranveer Chandra
summary: Checklist rubrics applied by large language model (LLM) judges have become a standard instrument for evaluating open-ended outputs and for rewarding them during training. Two assumptions surround this practice: that leniency or strictness is a property of the judge model, and that a rubric can be improved by asking a model to review it. We test both in a controlled grading task with planted flaws and on two human-labeled datasets, SummEdits and RAGTruth. Holding the judge and the outputs fixed, rubric content moves the pass rate of correct outputs from 2% to 100%, whereas changing the judge model or the rendering of the same checks moves it by a few points. Model self-review then drifts the rubric toward the reviser's own standard: it adds requirements the task never stated and deletes checks that human labels had taught, with three reviser models and on all three datasets. To measure and control this, we show that under all-must-pass aggregation the Shapley value of each check has an exact closed form, which yields per-check catch credit, false-fail blame and unique catches in linear time. Attribution shows that self-review deletes the checks that do unique work and keeps the checks that cause false fails. A change-control gate that combines these quantities with a provenance freeze on label-derived checks holds nearly every drifting revision chain at its starting quality, with identical decisions under three judge models.

title_html: ☆ DeGMatch: Target-Aware Reasoning Data Selection via Deconfounded Gradient Matching
authors_html: Changho Lee, Janghoon Han, Rajdeep Mukherjee, Yeda Song, Lening Nick Cui, Xinya Du, Honglak Lee
summary: Reasoning post-training on long trajectories has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but scaling such training to large datasets is increasingly expensive. We study target-aware reasoning data selection, where a small reference set specifies a target capability and guides the selection of training trajectories for specialization. We find that existing target-aware methods can exhibit limited target discrimination on long reasoning trajectories, while dominant population-level structure in candidate gradients can obscure finer target-dependent variation during gradient matching. To address these limitations, we introduce Deconfounded Gradient Matching (DeGMatch), which first constructs a target-relevance gate and then reranks candidates using model-specific gradients. DeGMatch centers gradients using the candidate-population mean and removes leading principal directions before target matching, reducing the influence of dominant population-level structure and improving target discrimination. Across mathematics, science, and code, DeGMatch outperforms strong heuristic, target-aware, and reasoning-specific data selection baselines, while remaining effective across selection budgets, model families, and scales. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/CHLee0801/degmatch.

title_html: ☆ Over-Defense in Coding Agents Begins at Silent Forks
authors_html: Hanjun Luo, Xuecheng Liu, Xiucheng Zhang, Zhuoning Xu, Yingbin Jin, Yankai Chen, Xue Liu, Hanan Salam
summary: Language models behind coding agents are post-trained with outcome rewards, and recent methods concentrate credit on the turns that decide the outcome. We find that defensive actions beyond what a task requires escape both. They begin at silent forks, the turns where every next action leads to the same outcome. Such actions leave the success rate unchanged, and frontier models take the disproportionate branch there in up to 91% of decisive actions under implicit budgets. The most direct fix, a checker in the trajectory reward, reaches these forks only through fully proportionate trajectories, leaving 74% of GRPO groups with identical rewards and behavior unchanged. This motivates a rethink of where learning signals belong, namely where behavior diverges, which a behavioral checker can locate and the outcome cannot. Our method, ForkDPO, contrasts a proportionate and a disproportionate action at the same prefix, at silent forks on both sides of the required behavior. On a test set of unseen repositories, it lowers a 4B model's disproportionate behavior from 70.3% to 58.9%, against 67.7% for DPO at randomly chosen turns, establishing behavioral divergence as a learning signal for how agents act beyond whether they finish. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Astarojth/silent-forks.

title_html: ☆ Epi: Towards a Persistent, Self-Improving Agent for Autonomous Research
authors_html: Yue Huang, Zhangchen Xu, Xiaonan Luo, Zheyuan Liu, Lichi Li, Yiping Wang, Peiyang Song, Eric Gabriel Ramos, Enze Xie, Olexandr Isayev, Paul Liang, Nouha Dziri, Huan Sun, Jianfeng Gao, Ying Liu, Misha Sra, Xiangliang Zhang, Alex Pentland, Zichen Chen
summary: We present \'{E}pi, an autonomous research agent that sustains investigations across model sessions and evolves its methods through accumulated experience. \'{E}pi combines persistent research history, hierarchical memory, branching and independent review to maintain research continuity, learn from experiments, and explore and revisit alternative approaches. Its experiments run across session boundaries, and a fixed verifier evaluates their outputs. \'{E}pi produced 120 record-setting results, comprising 20 numerical bound records across 12 families and 100 construction records across eight families. These include an approximately 84-fold narrower interval for the $n$-queens constant and a more than 3.6-million-fold narrower rigorous interval for the quartic Feigenbaum attractor dimension. Exact dual certificates establish that the Cohn-Elkies linear-programming bound cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11. Beyond numerical improvements, \'{E}pi gives a computer-assisted proof of Tuza's conjecture for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three triangle-active neighborhood types, with arbitrary multiplicities. We extend this research process to algorithmic coding with \'{E}pi-turbo, a lightweight configuration that develops executable solvers for tasks including vehicle routing, scheduling and production planning. On 30 FrontierOR tasks, \'{E}pi-turbo achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than Codex at 64% of its model cost, using the same underlying model and reasoning effort. \'{E}pi is designed to support human understanding by connecting computational results to explicit methods and mathematical arguments that researchers can examine and build upon.
comment: 23 pages, 7 figures. Technical report

title_html: ☆ What Can't Jev Decide? Probing the Limits of One-Pass Decision Models
authors_html: Wang Yang, Xinpeng Li, Yanyan Zhang, Chuang Ma, Shouren Wang, Jianzhe Wei, Liqin Ye, Xiaoran Cai, Mohsen Hariri, Vipin Chaudhary, Xiaotian Han
summary: Jev and its open replicas choose among the options a caller supplies with a single forward pass, fast enough to decide inside an agent loop. We ask what such a model cannot decide, and find a simple limit: Jev cannot make a decision that an LLM makes only by writing out intermediate steps. On a benchmark that varies one factor at a time, Jev finds and selects records without error up to 20k tokens and 64 options, but once the answer depends on two or more updates of one user, accuracy falls, to 53-80% at sixteen updates, because similar records interfere. Given a stale summary of the state, Jev follows it. On real decision items graded by how many thinking tokens a reference LLM needs, Jev answers 97.5% of the items that one forward pass of that LLM solves, but only 74% of the others. Jev also does not know its limit: its confidence flags the errors it makes itself but not those it inherits from a stale input, and neither an explicit nor a trained hand-off option catches the latter. The open models we evaluate share these limits. Checking the state such models rely on requires a model that reasons.

title_html: ☆ How Well Can LLMs Verbalize Mathematical Formulas? A Multi-Domain Evaluation
authors_html: Peter Volbach, Tim Schlippe
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across natural language tasks. But their ability to generate accurate written verbalizations of mathematical formulas has not been systematically evaluated. Such verbalization is important for text-to-speech systems supporting audio-based learning and visually impaired users. We evaluated five state-of-the-art LLMs across six scientific domains and constructed Read-Aloud Math, a balanced multi-domain corpus with LaTeX formulas, manually validated simple and extended transcriptions, multiple variants, textual context, domain labels, and formula complexity levels. Using multi-reference BLEU, GPT-5.2 achieved the highest score for simple transcriptions (75.9% without context, 64.9% with context), although without context it did not significantly outperform Grok 4.1 Fast or Claude Sonnet 4.5. Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieved the highest score for extended transcriptions without context (36.5%), and Grok 4.1 Fast with context (48.8%). For extended transcriptions, Statistics and Mathematics scored highest across the two context settings, while Physics scored lowest. Formula length was significantly negatively associated with BLEU for simple transcriptions without context, but not with context, whereas BLEU increased significantly with formula length for extended transcriptions in both settings. Grouping symbols were most frequently involved in transcription differences, while variable names, capitalization, and Greek letters were associated with lower BLEU scores. Overall, LLM-based formula verbalization is promising but remains sensitive to transcription type, textual context, and formula characteristics.
comment: Published in the IEEE Proceedings of the 3rd International Conference on Foundation and Large Language Models (FLLM 2026), Barcelona, Spain, November 17-20, 2026

title_html: ☆ Compositional Activation Steering Across Languages and Behaviors with Contextual Gates
authors_html: Daniil Gurgurov, Akansh Maurya, Josef van Genabith, Simon Ostermann, Hitomi Yanaka
summary: Activation steering has emerged as an effective and precise way to influence the behaviours of language models. However, composing multiple steering directions to control several behaviours simultaneously remains challenging, particularly in multilingual settings and with training-free steering vectors. We address this challenge with contextual steering, jointly training gates that adapt the strength of fixed steering directions to the current hidden state and interactions between interventions. Across a broad range of languages, behavioural attributes, and models, our approach outperforms constant-strength steering and four strong baselines, including prompting. It also better preserves general knowledge and keeps the model's internal computation closer to that of the prompted model. Our analysis further shows how jointly trained gates adapt their contributions during composition, explaining the mechanisms underlying effective compositional steering.

title_html: ☆ LastWords: Boring Problems Revisited
authors_html: Huayang Li, Richard Sproat
summary: In 2022, the second author published a Last Words piece in Computational Linguistics in which he pointed out that, despite the advances in AI up to that point, there were still some problems in natural language processing that on the one hand seemed trivial and perhaps boring, but on the other were hard to solve using purely neural methods. One such problem discussed in that context was text normalization, and a particular subproblem of that, namely number name reading. The piece came out just a few months before the first release of ChatGPT, and needless to say, a lot has happened since then. Indeed, as we document here, the problem (of number name reading) has practically been solved, at least by one of the latest frontier models. However, we believe that there are still open issues for such limited domain, constrained and limited resource problems, and that in some future machine learning approach, the massive resources of the latest frontier models would not be needed to solve them.
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure

title_html: ☆ Measuring Data Diversity with Embeddings: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Diversity Measures
authors_html: Cantao Su, Anna Wegmann, Esther Ploeger, Dong Nguyen
summary: Diversity is a critical property of text corpora, with direct implications for training data curation, test set design, and model generalization. However, its measurement remains fragmented and poorly understood. Existing embedding-based diversity measures vary widely in how they are computed and can yield substantially different diversity scores on the same data, yet no systematic comparison of their empirical behaviour exists. We make two contributions toward addressing this gap. First, we present a taxonomy of 21 embedding-based diversity measures, organizing them into four families based on their underlying computations. Second, we introduce EmbDivBench, a benchmark that evaluates these measures along three conceptually distinct components (variety, balance and disparity) on both simulated and natural text data. Although Mean Pairwise Distance is the most commonly used measure, our experiments show that it is outperformed by several alternatives on the three diversity components, with Graph Entropy being the best choice overall. Lastly, we distil these findings into practical recommendations for diversity measure selection.
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main). Code and data: this https URL

title_html: ☆ Learning to Program Retrievals: Composing Search Primitives via Reinforcement Learning
authors_html: Kyuyoung Kim, Zilin Xiao, Zhiyuan Wang, Avinash Atreya, Ke Yang, Jinwoo Shin, Kecheng Hao
summary: Retrieval-augmented language models increasingly use multi-step search to solve knowledge-intensive tasks, yet existing systems typically expose retrieval through fixed pipelines or collections of atomic tools. We introduce Retrieval Program Learning (RPL), a programmable search framework that allows a policy to compose search primitives into executable programs with local state and control flow. This enables adaptive search that can retrieve broadly, process intermediate results, and selectively construct model context without tying retrieval breadth to context consumption. However, the resulting flexibility creates a difficult exploration problem: useful programs may require several coordinated decisions, while reinforcement learning often supplies only sparse feedback. To address this challenge, we propose program mutation, a grammar-constrained and execution-verified procedure that generates local variants of suboptimal programs sampled during RL, converts them into training trajectories, and distills them back into the policy. We evaluate RPL on open-domain question answering and corpus-level reasoning tasks, comparing it with a range of retrieval and reasoning baselines. RPL consistently improves open-domain QA performance across model sizes and in- and out-of-domain benchmarks, with particularly large gains on multi-hop tasks. Notably, a 4B model trained with RPL outperforms all 8B model baselines. On corpus-level reasoning, RPL achieves the highest answer F1 and document-coverage F1 for both model sizes while substantially reducing context consumption and retrieval turns. Our results show that programmable search expands the retrieval strategies that agents can learn, while program mutation provides an effective mechanism for exploring useful program structures beyond direct on-policy sampling.

title_html: ☆ MisleadQA: Diagnosing LLM Failures under Misleading Context
authors_html: Hui Wang, Bohao Chu, Qianli Wang, Shuning Zhang, Norbert Fuhr
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer questions from retrieved or user-provided context. However, provided context can be factually true yet out-of-scope, describing a different entity, time, or location from the one the question targets, and still lead models to a wrong answer. Prior work has mainly studied factually false or irrelevant context. It remains unclear whether such out-of-scope context misleads models as much as false context, and whether adding gold context prevents models from being misled by either. We introduce **MisleadQA**, a diagnostic dataset of multiple-choice questions with an abstention option. Each question pairs gold context (G) with true but out-of-scope context (S) and false but in-scope context (F) supporting the same wrong answer. We evaluate six open-weight LLMs. On questions they answer correctly without context, providing S alone leads them to switch to this wrong answer in 29.3% of cases, and providing F alone does so in 75.4%. Adding G nearly removes the effect of S, but F still misleads models in 21.0% of cases, especially when F comes first. A context-faithful instruction reduces these errors mainly through abstention and lowers accuracy even with G. These findings suggest that evaluations should check whether context applies to the question, not only whether it is true, and should report correct, misled, and abstention rates together. Data and code are available at [https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MisleadQA](https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MisleadQA).

title_html: ☆ Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts
authors_html: Anna Pramod
summary: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. We show that this figure is measured in English and does not transfer. Across a 131k-sentence corpus spanning eleven Indic scripts, TinyLlama-1.1B's tokeniser emits 1.34 subword tokens per Latin-script word and 22.60 per Kannada word. This is not inefficiency; it is absence. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. The binding constraint is the vocabulary, not the parameter count. The consequence is concrete: on a 2048-token context window, the same model gives an English user 1,528 words of usable context and a Kannada user 91.

title_html: ☆ Ask, Don't Guess: Targeted Clarification for Speech Recognition Errors
authors_html: Sankalp Parashar, Preethi Jyothi, Sunita Sarawagi
summary: Speech recognition in real time in far-field conversational settings still incurs significant errors. Identifying potential error spans during streaming ASR permits a recourse mechanism where the speaker can be asked to repeat the affected content under cleaner acoustic conditions. We propose PARDON, a new framework for online error localization, that identifies spans likely to benefit from this intervention. Our supervision uses clean audio to estimate how the recognizer's output might change under improved acoustic conditions. We probabilistically align noisy and clean decodes using a pair-HMM to obtain soft supervision. These soft targets train a counterfactual gain scorer by combining a suite of acoustic and language features to produce token-level scores, that are further grouped into spans for targeted recourse. An LLM uses the ASR transcript of the repetition to revise only the selected span. At a precision of 70%, PARDON achieves the highest recall by identifying up to 52% more erroneous tokens compared to the strongest baseline. Targeted repetition yields relative WER reductions of up to 24% under a budget that accounts for both interruption frequency and the lengths of re-uttered spans.

title_html: ☆ Table Serialization Determines Which Relations Language Models Preserve
authors_html: Junwei Ma, Arun Kumar Chithanar, Palash Goyal, Chul Lee
summary: We study how text serialization affects table lookup in instruction-tuned language models. Our diagnostic asks the model to find the row containing a specified value under one named column, then return the value under another named column in that same row. We render the same synthetic 256-cell tables in row-major form and in column-major form with each header placed beside its values, while varying the table aspect ratio across five shapes. Across three models, the better format changes with table shape: row-major performs better on tall tables, whereas column-major performs better on wide tables. At 64 x 4, row-major leads by 42.3-54.0 percentage points; at 4 x 64, column-major leads by 35.0-59.0 points. Mapping wrong answers back to their source cells reveals a complementary error pattern: row-major tends to preserve the correct row but lose the target column, while column-major tends to preserve the correct column but lose the row. We use the term relational locality to describe this pattern: serialization keeps one relation locally available while making the other depend on positional alignment. A separate non-tabular ordering experiment supports this interpretation. Thus, apparent width-related failures in text-serialized tables depend on linearization, not table shape alone.

title_html: ☆ Who Gets Unmasked? Sampler-Induced Bias in Diffusion Language Models
authors_html: Xujun Che, Farsheed Haque, Depeng Xu, Xi Niu, Haopeng Zhang
summary: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate by gradually unmasking a canvas, so their samplers decide not only which token to write but also when to commit it. We show that this second decision changes who appears in generated text, a sampler-induced bias on top of the model's own. Common commit rules, including LLaDA's default, commit the positions whose sampled tokens are most probable; this peeking favors majority options. To separate the sampler from the model, we read the model's belief about a fork, such as a protagonist's gender, in one forward pass, and show that this belief matches exact sampling from the model. Measured against it, peeking samplers on LLaDA and Dream amplify occupational gender stereotypes and collapse opinion distributions, and confidence-based ordering shifts gender-balanced occupations toward men, more so under faster parallel decoding. We propose Fork-First Sampling, which decides the fork before anything else is written: it follows the belief or any target distribution, improves fluency, and avoids the stories that remark on the protagonist's gender, which prompt-based fixes produce, at the cost of one forward pass. Fairness evaluations of dLLMs should report the commit rule.

title_html: ☆ ECHO: Efficient Causal Self-Recursion Beyond Auxiliary Multi-Token Prediction
authors_html: Yuxuan Zhou, Junyuan Shang, Tianyu Wang, Chunrui Zheng, Zichang Liu, Wenbin Chang, Shuohuan Wang, Dianhai Yu
summary: Existing Multi-token prediction (MTP) methods are auxiliary by design: the multi-horizon loss mostly trains modules attached to the backbone, and each added horizon costs another module and another pass. We propose Efficient Causal Self-Recursion (ECHO), which removes both costs. The backbone's own final layer predicts every horizon, so the supervision lands on the parameters that generate the next token, and Dynamic Depth Sampling (DDS) keeps deeper horizons affordable by drawing the training depth with probabilities that decay along depth. Future prediction thus becomes part of the autoregressive objective rather than a task attached to it, and the gains follow on both sides of it. In pretraining, added depth converts into downstream accuracy where auxiliary modules saturate, concentrating on reasoning and code at half the MTP training overhead of training every depth. At inference, the pretrained model is its own drafter: it drafts beyond the depth it was trained for, and keeps its draft-target alignment on the open-ended, high-entropy generation where post-hoc drafters lose theirs. The advantage survives a doubled token budget, a repeated pretraining run, and supervised finetuning.

title_html: ☆ BanglaBBQ: A Bias Benchmark for Question Answering in the Bangladeshi Context
authors_html: Sumit Anthony Gomes, Yasin Rahman, Taeeba Tasnia, Faiza Nooren Suhita
summary: This paper introduces BanglaBBQ, a question-answering bias benchmark designed to capture stereotypes grounded in the Bangladeshi context, in both Bangla and English. Following KoBBQ and PakBBQ, BanglaBBQ adapts the original Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) by classifying its templates into three groups: directly translated (DT), modified to align target groups or contexts with Bangladesh (TM), and removed when deemed unsuitable for the Bangladeshi context (SR). This process retains 140 templates across six categories, comprising 76 DT and 64 TM templates. Five newly authored (NA) categories, based on stereotypes common in Bangladeshi society, are then added: marital status, age and political perception, regional origin, educational background, and mental-health status. Native Bangladeshi annotators judged all 466 newly authored templates, and 372 were retained because a strict majority of English annotators identified the intended target and rated the attitude as common enough. Each newly authored template is linked to a documented source and a verbatim quote from it. Each evaluated template also has a counter-stereotypical version of its disambiguated context. The dataset was evaluated using two open-weight models (Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B) and two closed models (GPT-4.1-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash). All four lean towards the stereotyped person when the context is ambiguous, in both languages, and the effect of language differs by model, so English results do not predict behaviour in Bangla. On the adapted BBQ templates, both Qwen3 models are also less accurate when the context contradicts a stereotype than when it confirms it. On the newly authored templates, the closed models follow counter-stereotypical evidence almost perfectly, and all four models are more biased on the templates that annotators validated than on those they rejected.

title_html: ☆ GLOSS-MT: Controllable Low-Resource Machine Translation with an Editable Dictionary
authors_html: Mich-Seth Owusu, Stephen E. Moore, Akwasi Asare, Lawrence Adu Gyamfi, Paul Azunre, Joel Budu, Jonathan Asiamah
summary: Adapting a pretrained machine translation (MT) model to new terminology usually requires new parallel data and another round of fine-tuning, which is costly for low-resource languages. We ask whether controllability can be added to MT, and the fine-tuning burden reduced, without degrading the pretrained model. GLOSS-MT looks up the source's noun phrases in an offline English-Twi dictionary, replaces every phrase found by its Twi translation in place, and fine-tunes a translation model once to translate these mixed inputs. We apply the same data and pipeline to NLLB-200 (600M, 1.3B, 3.3B), OPUS-MT en-tw and TranslateGemma 4B. On a document-level English-to-Asante Twi benchmark (84 documents, four domains), every fine-tune scores above its pretrained base in chrF2 (+2.85 to +5.48), and the three NLLB fine-tunes are the best open systems (50.12-50.80). A direct controllability test on human-translated Bible passages shows that the three fine-tunes tested write 79-97% of the dictionary terms, and that replacing every dictionary entry by a different term changes the output accordingly (70-97% of the new terms appear) with no retraining. We release the models, data and code.

title_html: ☆ PV-Decoding: Progressive Verification Decoding with Decode Gating for Diffusion Language Models
authors_html: Renxi Liu, Yiming Li, Shengyin Sun, Chen Chen, Xian Wang, Shuai Yang, Huiling Zhen, Xianzhi Yu, Yaoyuan Wang, Weizhe Lin, Xiaosong Li
summary: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer an attractive alternative to autoregressive generation by updating multiple tokens in parallel, but their inference efficiency is still limited by the cost of safely committing tentative predictions. In particular, speculative decoding for dLLMs is challenging because speculative tokens within the same diffusion block may depend on one another, making aggressive acceptance prone to error propagation and strict verification computationally expensive. We present PV-Decoding, a confidence-driven speculative decoding framework with progressive verification for block diffusion inference. PV-Decoding partitions masked positions into directly decoded tokens, speculative tokens, and unresolved tokens using two confidence thresholds, and then verifies speculative tokens with progressively stronger policies, including single-batch, dual-batch, and multi-batch verification. This design exposes a practical accuracy--efficiency trade-off: weaker verification minimizes overhead, whereas stronger verification improves acceptance precision and robustness. Experiments on three diffusion language models across GSM8K, MBPP, and HumanEval show that PV-Decoding reduces sequential model forward passes (MFPs) by 8%--37% relative to confidence-based decoding, while keeping the largest observed accuracy drop to 1.3%. On Dream-7B-Instruct/GSM8K, PV-Decoding (1-batch) and PV-Decoding (2-batch) improve throughput by 7.0%--13.6% under the same hardware budget, whereas PV-Decoding (multi-batch) is slower under the current runtime. These results suggest that confidence-guided speculation with structured verification is a practical path toward efficient and reliable dLLM inference.

title_html: ☆ DiffuPlan: Editable Planning State for Diffusion Language Model Agents
authors_html: Qisheng Zhou, Zhen Xiong, Qiaoyu Tan
summary: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) are emerging as an alternative to autoregressive (AR) language models, yet dLLM agents largely inherit an interaction protocol designed for AR generation: once intermediate state is written, later observations can only be incorporated by appending more text. This is a poor match to a defining capability of dLLMs -- reconstructing earlier text conditioned on context that appears both before and after it. We ask whether this capability can support a different agent-state paradigm in which intermediate planning state is directly revisable as evidence arrives. We introduce DiffuPlan, a diffusion search agent that maintains a single editable planning state and reconstructs only the affected steps when later evidence resolves an entity or changes the search route. To support variable-length revisions, we introduce Expansion-Partition Marginalization (EPM), which marginalizes over equivalent expansion paths. We further adapt diffusion trajectory RL to multi-turn search. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, DiffuPlan achieves 50.24 average F1, outperforming strong AR search agents. More importantly, under identical data and training, editable planning state improves the diffusion agent by 2.44 F1 versus only 0.47 for its AR source model. These results show that dLLMs need not imitate append-only AR agents: revising committed state is a distinct agentic advantage.

title_html: ☆ When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
authors_html: Yichuan Chen, Xin Wang
summary: Language models sometimes repeat verbatim until the generation limit. We study the exit rather than the entrance: given that a span has already been repeated $n$ times, when is escape still possible? Along the loop the context is deterministic, so loop survival under any sampler can be computed exactly from one forward pass. Pure sampling leaves a positive escape probability at every step; top-$p$ with threshold $\pi>1/2$ locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches $\pi$. A bounded penalty can leave a position locked; a penalty that outgrows the model's preference for the loop over unseen tokens guarantees escape under top-$p$. The same analysis predicts a blind spot in the widely deployed DRY sampler: its sequence breakers cap the penalty at $\lambda b^{g-1-a}$ for loops whose longest breaker-free run has $g$ tokens. On eleven open models, 66\% of locked units with $g=6$ stay locked under DRY and 1\% with $g=8$. In free generation with llama.cpp, all 109 loops that survive DRY have $g\le 7$. We propose DRY-C, which adds a term that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, up to its look-back window. With it, none of 720 structured-output generations looped to the length limit, and task completion stayed close to DRY's.

title_html: ☆ Do Conversational Agents Need Explicit Memory? A Controlled Comparison with Raw-History Retrieval
authors_html: Yongjie Zhou, Shuai Wang, Bevan Koopman, Guido Zuccon
summary: Explicit memory systems transform conversation history into persistent representations intended to improve future access, often at substantial construction cost. Yet it remains unclear whether this added complexity yields better answer accuracy than retrieving directly from raw history. This study compares six state-of-the-art explicit memory systems with raw-history RAG on LongMemEval-S and BEAM-100K under original and controlled retrieval settings. We find only localized gains for particular question types and tight run-time context budgets, with no consistent advantage over strong raw-history RAG baselines. Oracle retrieval shows that some systems fail to preserve answer-supporting information during explicit memory construction, while others preserve it but fail to retrieve it effectively, despite construction costs reaching hours per conversation. Our findings suggest that while many existing memory systems for AI agents emphasize increasingly elaborate explicit memory construction, they are often evaluated without strong controlled comparisons to raw-history RAG and may underemphasize retrieval. Retrieval remains a major bottleneck when useful information is preserved, suggesting that improving access to existing information may be at least as important as constructing richer explicit memory.

title_html: ☆ What RL Brings to Reasoning: A Few Decisions the Base Model Would Not Make
authors_html: Siyu Zhang, Yuquan Lu, Yoshua Y. Li, Yifan Ding, Kun Zeng, Yu Huo, Yifu Guo, Rongxiang Weng, Xunliang Cai, Xiaoying Tang
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) substantially improves mathematical reasoning, but what it adds to the base model remains unclear. We investigate this through a sequence of generation-time interventions on Qwen3-4B-Base, measuring how much of its RL-trained counterpart's gain each intervention recovers on 120 AIME problems. Power sampling with the same 8,192-token output limit brings no gain beyond greedy decoding. Yet borrowing the RL model's token only where the two models' greedy choices differ, roughly 4% of generated positions, recovers 90.5% of the pass@1 gain, with similar recovery across three model pairs on MATH-500. We find that even a single opening token has a substantial effect: forcing the base model to begin with "Alright" recovers 35% of the RL gain. The opening alone is insufficient, however. Later replacements after the same opening add another 5.2 percentage points to pass@1, and the fixed rules we test for inserting reflective words such as "Wait" do not reproduce this benefit. Sparse replacement also retains much of the base model's diversity while staying close to the RL model at pass@1. At k=256, it solves 67.5% of the problems, significantly more than the RL model (61.4%) and a mixture of whole responses matched in pass@1 (61.45%). The comparison is at equal attempt counts rather than equal compute, since rl-replace consults both models at every decoding step. These results show that the opening can recover a meaningful part of the RL gain, but a larger contribution comes from later choices, which can be borrowed while retaining much of the base model's diversity. Code is available at https://github.com/CyrusZhang04/WhatRLBrings.

title_html: ☆ Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model
authors_html: Arash Ebrahim Abtahizadeh, Muna Aghamelu, Adil Ahmed, Juan C. Angeles Acuna, Alexis Audran-Reiss, Asaf Avrahamy, Yoram Bachrach, Can Balioglu, Amar Budhiraja, Onur Çelebi, Gaurav Chaurasia, Joy Chen, Lynn Cherif, Lucia Cipolina-Kun, Gal Cohen, Timothée Darcet, Beto de Paola, Digant Desai, Sam Devlin, Derek Dunfield, Ivan Evtimov, Maryam Fazel-Zarandi, Rob Fergus, Jean-Christophe Gagnon-Audet, Grant Gardner, Bhavul Gauri, Paris Giampouras, Sujan Kumar Gonugondla, Antoine Grosnit, Young Han, Michael Hassid, Monuril Islam, Masoud Jalili Sabet, Songhao Jia, Narine Kokhlikyan, Svetlana Kurtsman, Sandra Lefdal, Chee Hau Leow, Noam Levi, Mike Lewis, Sanae Lotfi, Xiyang Luo, Despoina Magka, Saeed Mahloujifar, Neal Mangaokar, Ishita Mediratta, Alexander H. Miller, Hela Momand, Saba Nazir, Kelvin Niu, Mattia Opper, Parth Pathak, Alberto Pepe, Danielle Pintz, Mikhail Plekhanov, Sidhartha Reddy Potu, Anton Protopopov, Shengyi Qian, Shashank Rajput, Joseph Rocca, Scott Roy, Luca Sbordone, Amin Shakeri, Tatiana Shavrina, Michael Shvartsman, Ruan Silva, Anya Sims, Eric Michael Smith, Hugo Touvron, Mabel Ubong, Isabel Urrego, Yanzheng Xiang, Zhiyuan Yao, Alex Yarmula, He Ye, Jade Yu, Luke Zettlemoyer, Arman Zharmagambetov, Perpetua Fathima Ahlijah, Tremo Ahmed, Enrique Alfonseca, Pedram Bashiri, Nikolay Bashlykov, Amine Benhalloum, Aaron Berman, Rohith Bhatia, Siddharth Bhattacharya, Prashant Bhende, Chloe Bi, Shuchao Bi, Clement Anthonioz Blanc, Allen Bolourchi, Iva Simon-Bubalo, Pere-Lluís Huguet Cabot, Andrea Caciolai, Erica Cai, Xiang Tony Cao, Yue Cao, Andrew Caples, Jinzhao Chang
summary: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

title_html: ☆ Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
authors_html: Chengyu Xie, Fei Shen, Shuyi Miao, Yue Feng, Jian Yu, Pengyang Shao, Yijun Tian, Xiaoyu Du
summary: The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. To address this, we analyze cross-lingual safety behavior at the neuron level and identify a compact set of safety-related neurons shared across languages, termed the safety kernel (SK). Specifically, we first utilize multilingual parallel safe and unsafe prompts to compute safety contrast with activation responsiveness (SCAR) scores, identifying language-wise safety-neuron candidates from internal activation patterns. We then intersect the resulting language-wise safety-neuron sets to obtain the SK, and validate its functional relevance to cross-lingual safety behavior through activation suppression and activation-state transfer interventions. Finally, building on the SK coordinates, we introduce SK-Masked LoRA, which constrains LoRA adaptation to the feed-forward network (FFN) output dimensions corresponding to the SK, thereby focusing safety-related changes on the cross-lingually shared neuron coordinates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SK-Masked LoRA substantially reduces attack success rates across multiple languages, including languages excluded from SK discovery, while intervening on only a small fraction of internal neuron coordinates and producing generally limited changes in the model's general capabilities.

title_html: ☆ Training with Ciphers to Enhance In-Context Terminology Learning For Translation from Rare Languages
authors_html: Deevyanshu Malu, Deeptanshu Malu, Sunita Sarawagi
summary: Fine-tuning LLMs with in-context examples (IC-Train) lets translation models adapt to new parallel data at deployment, but it is unclear whether they actually learn the translations of rare terms from those examples. We formalize this capability as in-context term learning (ICTL). We show that standard IC-Train develops this capability only weakly, and propose RareCipherFT, which strengthens it without any lexical resources. RareCipherFT pairs each training target with in-context examples that share a rare term with it. It then replaces that term with a character-shuffled cipher in both the context and the reference, so the term can only be recovered by copying from context. The ciphered fraction of training data is annealed to preserve translation quality. Across seven translation directions between English and Tamil, Assamese, Mizo, Nepali and Hausa, and four models from 1B to 7B parameters, RareCipherFT raises term recall over standard IC-Train by 5-15 absolute points without lowering COMET. Probes using synonyms, nonce words and controls for shared surface context show that these gains come from linking source terms to their in-context translations rather than from shortcuts.

title_html: ☆ From Stories to Features: Scaling Concept Vectors for AI Alignment & Interpretability
authors_html: Dmitry Scherbakov, Oleg Chernikov, Victoria Khamash, Kirill Afendulev, Alexey Dontsov, Ivan Oseledets, Elena Tutubalina, Anton Korznikov
summary: We study feature vectors: directions in a language model's activation space that correspond to human-interpretable concepts, such as honesty or deception. Existing unsupervised methods like sparse autoencoders attempt to recover the whole feature space, often at the cost of feature quality and interpretability. We take a more pragmatic route: focusing on concepts relevant to AI safety and alignment, we generate synthetic concept-antagonist story pairs and use the difference of their mean model activations as a feature vector. We scale this approach to 1,036 alignment-relevant concepts using 2M synthetic stories across multiple languages and genres, which we publicly release. Across six models from three model families, our feature vectors reliably generalize to detecting their corresponding concepts in chat dialogues and web text. They form an interpretable geometry shared across models and can causally steer model behavior when injected into activations. We further use these features to analyze model representations during jailbreak attacks, mathematical and agentic reasoning. Our targeted feature construction thus offers a scalable route to studying concepts in language models, potentially extending to millions of features across arbitrary domains.

title_html: ☆ EGIP: An Evidence-Grounded Interaction Protocol for Clinical Agents
authors_html: Zecheng Ren, Ruichen Cong, Yi Min Chen, Jing Zhang, Feiyang Chen, Wutong Zhang, Kaixiang Wang, Zihan Wang, Jiong Lou, Jie LI, Qun Jin
summary: Interactive clinical agents acquire evidence through patient dialogue and diagnostic examinations, yet their performance also depends on how the interaction environment exposes information, available actions, and examination results. When these conditions are implicit or inconsistently controlled, final-answer accuracy can conflate diagnostic reasoning with the effects of the interaction protocol. We propose the \textbf{E}vidence-\textbf{G}rounded \textbf{I}nteraction \textbf{P}rotocol (EGIP), which enforces role-specific information boundaries, exposes diagnostic actions without revealing their results, retrieves examination results from stored clinical records, and organizes acquired evidence for final decision-making. By separating evidence acquisition from terminal prediction, EGIP enables different decision strategies to operate on the same observations. We evaluate EGIP across two clinical-agent frameworks, five datasets, and six language models. EGIP improves diagnostic accuracy over native baselines across all primary comparisons. A clinician review further shows that the proportion of automatically scored correct responses jointly judged evidence-supported rises from 10.20\% to 36.55\%. These findings support the effectiveness of EGIP as a unified interaction protocol for improving clinical-agent performance through controlled evidence access and acquisition.

title_html: ☆ Backend-Frontend Converter: Component-Based Conversion of .NET Computational Models to TypeScript
authors_html: Petr Ivankov, Max Shestov
summary: Computational models developed in .NET often need to run locally within web applications. We present Backend--Frontend Converter, an architecture for generating TypeScript implementations of component-based models. The converter maps components, connections, aliases, and formula trees to model-specific TypeScript code. Reusable runtime libraries provide numerical integration, data access, and state handling. We evaluate stored generated implementations through four orbital scenarios and a recorded trading-strategy comparison. Orbital calculations execute in a browser and are paired with C\# results by crossing event and timestamp; trading outputs are aligned by date. Analytic scheduler tests and deliberately perturbed outputs assess the validation procedure. Each orbital scenario produces 91 paired events with identical timestamps. Position and velocity differences remain below $(10^{-6}\)~km$ and $(10^{-9}\)~km/s$. All 20 analytic scheduler checks pass, and the comparator detects each of three prescribed state and time perturbations. The trading comparison contains 501 aligned daily records with matching indicator values, positions, and order events. The evaluated implementations preserve the compared outputs across the C#/TypeScript boundary. Component-specific generation and reusable execution libraries provide a practical route from supported .NET computational models to TypeScript applications.

title_html: ☆ Vocal-Tract Acoustics, Aerodynamics, and Overlap-and-Add Synthesis in DYNARTmo
authors_html: Bernd J. Kröger
summary: This paper presents the acoustic and aerodynamic extension of DYNARTmo, a dynamic articulatory model for visualizing and synthesizing speech production. Gestural control trajectories determine vocal-tract geometry, which is converted into an acoustic tube with nasal branching and effective lateral passages. A lumped aerodynamic network relates prescribed glottal motion and pulmonary pressure to airflow and supraglottal pressure storage. Phonatory excitation, oral friction, and glottal aspiration are synthesized as separate contributions. Frame-specific acoustic responses are combined by overlap-and-add, preserving response tails beyond individual control frames. Three German words, ``Tasse'', ``Muse'', and ``Lade'', illustrate the coordination of articulation, pressure, flow, and acoustic sources across vowels, nasals, laterals, fricatives, and plosives. The implementation has been optimized by the author primarily for sound recognizability; independent perceptual evaluation remains outstanding, and fricative-noise naturalness requires further refinement. The model provides an inspectable, articulatorily controlled production plant for future neural simulations of babbling, imitation, and early word acquisition. Further work will improve acoustic realism, reduce empirical source corrections, and extend the sensory information available to developmental learning models.

title_html: ☆ Modeling Discourse Profiles in Climate Misinformation Discourse
authors_html: Ge Gao, Zhengyang Shan, Bryan A. Plummer, Margrit Betke, Derry Wijaya
summary: Prior work on climate misinformation detection typically classifies individual comments or claims using text alone. This framing overlooks a key property of online climate discourse: misinformation is often produced, reinforced, and sustained through recurring rhetorical patterns that reappear across comments and threads. Using a large-scale TikTok climate discourse dataset, we construct discourse profiles by clustering climate-related comments into recurring rhetorical patterns. We then incorporate these profiles into fine-grained climate misinformation classifiers using a late-fusion architecture. Under video-disjoint evaluation across three training seeds, discourse-profile-aware models significantly improve macro-F1 over text-only baselines for bag-of-words, TF-IDF, and MPNet representations. RoBERTa-large exhibits a positive mean improvement but substantially greater variability, and the difference is not statistically significant. Beyond classification, our results show discourse profiles shape misinformation reception and propagation. Discourse-profile-conditioned language model agents exhibit misinformation acceptance patterns aligned with profile-level misinformation prevalence in ClimateDisc, and the relationship between misinformation prevalence and engagement persistence differs across dominant discourse profiles.

title_html: ☆ Write Once, Check Many: Reusable Ledgers for Post-Hoc Policy Compliance Auditing of Agent Trajectories
authors_html: Ashwin Nagarajan, Gursimran Panesar, Alicia Yang, Mona T. Diab, Virginia Smith, Aashiq Muhamed
summary: Auditing LLM agents against policies is critical to ensure safety but requires rereading long trajectories once per policy. Can we instead record each trajectory once and reuse that record for policies not known in advance? We propose write once, check many, a framework in which a writer model converts each agent trajectory into a policy-independent ledger of the agent's actions and outcomes. A reader then checks each new policy against the ledger alone, without access to the original trajectory. On 900 trajectories from SHADE-Arena, $\tau$-bench, and $\tau^2$-bench, we show that a 12B reader of narrative ledgers can either match or in fact achieve higher AUC than the same 12B model reading full trajectories. On SHADE-Arena policies that combine several facts, our approach outperforms a 31B model reading the trajectory (.777 vs. .713 AUC). When checking eight SHADE-Arena policies separately, ledgers use about $5\times$ fewer tokens, including the cost of writing them. A deeper analysis shows that rule-based extraction performs better on some single-action policies, and ledgers can miss evidence in long tool outputs and message contents. Our results suggest that reusable, policy-independent records can make retrospective agent auditing more efficient and effective, and highlight important considerations in ledger design.

title_html: ☆ Ben-Misandry: A Bengali Dataset and Late-Fusion Transformer Framework for Detecting Anti-Male Gender Hate
authors_html: Md Mehedi Hasan Nipu, Chinmoy Mitra, Tarannum Ahmed Nowshin, Israt Moyeen Noumi
summary: Gender based hate speech research in Bengali has focused almost exclusively on misogyny, leaving anti male hate, or misandry, entirely unstudied for this language and creating a systematic blind spot in moderation systems trained to catch attacks on women but not on men. We introduce Ben-Misandry, the first Bengali misandry detection dataset: 5,000 comments across six taxonomy classes, including a novel category for mocking male emotional vulnerability with no direct analogue in existing misogyny taxonomies. The corpus is taxonomy-controlled synthetic data generated with GPT-4.1, spot-checked by four human reviewers on a 500-comment sample who confirmed the large majority of assigned labels; a full inter-annotator- agreement study is left to future work. We benchmark it with a classical pipeline (seven classifiers over four text representations) and a transformer pipeline (BanglaBERT, XLM-RoBERTa, and two fusion strategies). The best classical model, a linear SVM over character-level TF-IDF, reaches 91.8% accuracy; a late fusion ensemble averaging BanglaBERT and XLM-RoBERTa softmax outputs reaches 96.6% accuracy and macro ROC-AUC above 99%, nominally ahead of every single model and early fusion, though we have not run significance testing to confirm these margins are meaningful. We relate this to classifier combination theory, under which averaging encoders with decorrelated errors is expected to reduce variance, and corroborate the decision boundary with Shapley explanations that recover the same class- discriminative vocabulary found in our exploratory analysis, while noting this cannot rule out the model partly keying on synthetic-generation artifacts. Our results indicate misandry detection in Bengali is feasible and measurable on this synthetic corpus, offered as an initial public resource pending validation on real-world data.

title_html: ☆ Which Long Documents Matter? A Controlled Study of Data Selection for Context Extension
authors_html: Junlong Jia, Jiang Zhou, Xing Wu, Chaochen Gao Tinghao Yu, Feng Zhang, Lilin Wang
summary: Natural long documents are widely used for context extension, but which selection pipelines are effective remains unclear. We conduct a controlled comparison on Qwen2.5-3B at 128K under matched 6B-token continued-training budgets. Random sampling of natural long documents (random-long) outperforms repacking at longer evaluation lengths. Within the same candidate pool, selecting documents with high LongPPL key-token density yields further gains, unlike the evaluated generic-quality and LLM-judge selectors. We introduce truncLongPPL to reduce scoring cost by computing key-token density over a truncated prefix. At 128K, scoring the first half of the reference span yields downstream performance close to full-span scoring with a measured $2.28\times$ end-to-end scoring speedup. Across three training seeds, truncLongPPL achieves the highest mean scores among evaluated pipelines, exceeding random-long by 4.54 points on validation HELMET and 3.28 on held-out RULER, with gains most consistent in retrieval. At a 256K target context, it gains 2.82 average RULER points over random-long on Qwen2.5-3B. In short/long mixed training across Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen3-8B, and OLMo~3-7B, it gains 1.47--7.31 average RULER points over random-long mixing, with seven-task short-context averages within 0.23 points of the corresponding baselines. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), Qwen3-8B and OLMo~3-7B models trained with selected long documents outperform their random-long counterparts by 1.13--1.67 points on LongBench v2 and 0.62--1.44 points on MRCR.

title_html: ☆ When Opposite Premises Translate Identically: A Source-Conditioned Diagnostic for Multilingual Commonsense Items
authors_html: Shuai Wang, Rui Hu
summary: Multilingual reasoning comparisons depend on translated premises preserving the relations in their English sources. Automatic translation scores can rank source-target pairs, but an acceptance decision alone cannot certify a counterfactual benchmark field. We test a source-contrast diagnostic for ACCORD premises: reverse the English polarity, translate both arms independently, count identical target outputs, and score each arm against its own source. Across 71 matched question identities at two containing-item depths, five target languages, and three translation checkpoints, Swahili has 63, 113, and 67 exact collisions among 710 pairs per checkpoint. At a human-reference-calibrated threshold, round-trip NLI passes both arms of 3 of the 113 NLLB-3.3B collisions, while LaBSE passes 78. Each collision proves at least one unfaithful translation, but does not identify its arm. These controlled measurements do not establish screening accuracy on spontaneous translation errors or a language-by-hop reasoning effect; the study has no native equivalence labels or answer-model evaluation.

title_html: ☆ Toward a Universal Local Speech Feature Extractor Through Distillation
authors_html: Jessica Yang, Marcelo Beramendi Caballero, Ju-Chieh Chou, Karen Livescu
summary: Self-supervised speech models commonly consist of a set of convolutional neural network (CNN) layers used as a local feature extractor, followed by transformer layers. The CNN layers are computationally demanding, and are also similar across models and resemble the much simpler mel spectral features. We hypothesize that the CNN layers can be replaced by a simple, universal model. To test this hypothesis, we learn a two-layer feature extractor via distillation from one or more teacher models (HuBERT, data2vec, and WavLM). Experiments on SUPERB(-SG) benchmark tasks show that our model largely retains the performance of the teacher models and can also be used in an unseen model (wav2vec 2.0). Our feature extractor requires only 3% of the MACs of the CNNs, resulting in a $>$20% overall inference runtime reduction.

title_html: ☆ Ask Less, Ask Better: Allocating User Attention in Proactive LLM Agents with Interruption Budgets
authors_html: Xuanming Zhang, Amir H. Rezaeian, Miguel Ballesteros, Weiyi Sun, Werner Geyer, Lydia B. Chilton, Zhou Yu, Yassine Benajiba, Dan Roth
summary: LLM agents can ask clarifying questions to complete tasks, but answering each question demands users' time and effort. Existing evaluations typically measure this burden by counting questions, treating necessary and avoidable questions equally. We propose an evaluation protocol that distinguishes how often agents ask from how well they ask. An interruption budget limits the number of questions, while a user-attention cost charges extra for questions that are hard to read or not worth asking, as rated by a human-validated LLM judge. Beyond question counts, this cost captures perceived effort: on conversation pairs with the same number of questions, human annotators agreed with the cost on which conversation required more effort 75% of the time. Across eight LLMs and four customer-service domains, limiting agents to one to three questions reduces user-attention cost by 36-73% while keeping 86-94% of the task reward they earn with unlimited questions. At the same budget, reviewing each question against the memory of users' earlier answers cuts attention cost by another 13% with little reward loss and yields more valuable questions. Models also differ sharply in how well they ask: at the same user-attention cost, the most efficient models gain more than twice as much reward from their questions as the others. These results show that asking less and asking better are distinct goals, and that evaluations of proactive agents should measure both.

title_html: ☆ FlashMap: Flow Map Speculative Decoding
authors_html: Jeff Shen, Zhejian Zhou, Ryan Lee, Jonathan May, Shirley Ho
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight drafter to propose a block of tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel pass. Autoregressive drafters generate this block one token at a time, whereas block diffusion drafters such as DFlash generate it in one pass, making drafting faster. However, these diffusion drafters predict each token independently, ignoring dependencies between tokens in the block. We introduce FlashMap, a continuous flow drafter that conditions a flow map language model on the target model's hidden states and generates the whole block in one forward pass while capturing inter-token dependencies. On Qwen3-8B, FlashMap is faster than a matched DFlash baseline on every benchmark, with 7% higher average speedup and up to 6.1x lossless acceleration.

title_html: ☆ What Matters for NVFP4 Training? A Comparative Study of Low-Precision Pretraining Recipes
authors_html: Anjulie Agrusa, Andrei Panferov, Elizabeth Wei, Keith Wyss, Paul Gibbons, Erik Schultheis, Jinhang Choi, Frank Sun, Tijmen Blankevoort, Dan Alistarh
summary: Training large language models directly in 4-bit floating-point (FP) formats promises substantial improvements in throughput and energy efficiency. While some recipe design choices have been validated at scale, many promising approaches remain untested beyond small models and short token horizons, leaving open the question of which trends will hold. We present a systematic comparison of recent NVFP4 recipes at medium model scale, evaluating dense 8B and 30B-A3B MoE models trained for up to 1T tokens, with a focus on which ingredients are necessary for accuracy recovery. We propose a final recipe grounded in the principles behind established stable NVFP4 training at scale, incorporating state-of-the-art techniques such as unbiased gradient estimation with lower quantization error than stochastic rounding. To the best of our knowledge, this is the strongest FP4 training result demonstrated at this scale to date in loss gap to BF16. Through ablation studies, we find that: (i) each technique in the optimized recipe measurably improves loss trajectory, (ii) selective high-precision layers are necessary for recovering accuracy at scale, (iii) not all tensors in the backward pass benefit equally from de-biasing, leaving room to apply complementary error-reduction techniques to the remaining tensors.

title_html: ☆ Beyond Clean Accuracy: The Practical Challenges and Benefits of Pixel-Based Language Models
authors_html: Haowen Tang, Wei Xia, Raoyuan Zhao, Hinrich Schütze, Yihong Liu
summary: Pixel-based language models process rendered text without relying on a fixed subword vocabulary, offering a promising approach to noisy and multilingual inputs. However, their practical value depends on whether they can be reliably adapted to downstream tasks. To this end, we systematically examine this question through fine-tuning behavior, typographical robustness, and zero-shot crosslingual transfer. Under our tested settings, pixel-based models require longer training and broader labelled-data coverage than text-based models, while delayed learning and learning-rate-dependent failures make adaptation less reliable. Our analyses further suggest that task-relevant information is less readily accessible in pretrained pixel representations, placing greater demands on fine-tuning. Once successfully adapted, however, pixel-based models lose substantially less accuracy under typographical noise and achieve higher target-language accuracy than English-pretrained text-based counterparts on two crosslingual benchmarks, despite weaker clean English performance. Together, these findings reveal a central trade-off: replacing tokenization with rendering reduces sensitivity to corrupted and unfamiliar inputs, but shifts a central bottleneck to downstream adaptation.
